body: Three points where the spec's claims outrun its own evidence. (1) The entire study rests on FR-002's CodeBERT classifier, but the assumption that it 'can accurately distinguish LLM-generated code from human code' is asserted, not established: no source is given for the existence or validated accuracy of such a pre-trained classifier, and the ground-truth check (FR-007/SC-006, precision/recall ≥ 0.85 on a minimum-10-block subset) is both post-hoc and statistically far too small to bound classifier error at the level the matching pipeline requires. If the label is unreliable, every downstream comparison is confounded at the origin of the measurement. (2) The latency definition in FR-004 appears inverted: 'time from commit containing the bug fix to the resolution of the linked issue' measures post-fix administrative lag, not maintenance burden; the quantity of interest would run from block introduction (or bug report) to the fix commit. As written, SC-003 does not measure what it claims. (3) The methodology's shallow clone (depth=100, per the project description) is in tension with tracking six months of subsequent history; the spec never states how full post-introduction history will be obtained, and the edge-case handling of moved/refactored blocks ('if the file path hash changes or the directory level changes, the block is excluded') will systematically drop exactly the high-churn blocks most relevant to the churn outcome — a survivorship bias in the dependent variable itself.
